paras: The threatened lynching of Edmund Morrison followed the shooting of Henry Hunter, a young man of Athens, Georgia, at Carter's camp on the Georgia, Carolina and Northern railroad on the night of August 16, 1890, of which Morrison, a Black laborer at the camp, was accused. About 100 men with bloodhounds hunted Morrison, and wire reports carried across the country stated that he would be lynched when caught. He was instead captured by a sheriff and lodged in the Augusta jail to protect him from a mob, and in September he was tried, convicted and sentenced to hang.

Carter's camp lay on the works of the railroad about nine miles from Athens, according to the Savannah Morning News, or about eight, according to the Athens wire. Hunter was described as managing a line of drays for his uncle, Samuel Hunter, while the Augusta dispatch called him a clerk in the store where Morrison was employed. The Morning News's Athens correspondent wrote that Hunter had reproved a man "for whipping a mule until blood came" and received an insolent reply.

That night, by the same correspondent's account, Morrison came to the door of the commissary store, asked Hunter whether he meant what he had said at noon, and, when Hunter said he did, shot him in the left temple and ran. Hunter died about one o'clock the next morning.

A posse left Athens on the night of the shooting, and bloodhounds put on the trail followed it only "with great difficulty." The Morning News printed a description of Morrison, said to hail from Memphis, as five feet six inches tall and "a burly, determined villain." According to the Athens wire, the dogs followed him through two counties, about 100 men were on his track, and "if caught he will be lynched."

On August 18 Sheriff Weir of Clarke County and Press Elder captured Morrison near Madison, and Weir took him by train to Augusta "for safekeeping." An Augusta dispatch said he was jailed there to protect him from a mob and that Hunter's friends would have taken him from the sheriff and hanged him if they had had the chance. No report of an attempt on Morrison or on the jail appears in the coverage.

Morrison was tried in Madison superior court on September 4 in a trial that ran from nine to two o'clock, and the jury found him guilty without recommendation to mercy. Judge Lumpkin sentenced him to be hanged on October 17. A follow-up item from Athens timed the arguments and the jury's deliberation and called it "one of the quickest trials on record."

In Georgia, the Savannah Morning News followed the case in its own Athens and Augusta dispatches under headlines running from "AN ATHENIAN SHOT BY A NEGRO" to "HUNTER'S MURDERER CAUGHT" and "BOOKED FOR THE GIBBET," calling Morrison the murderer well before his trial.

Outside the state, the Athens wire ran on August 18 and 19 under headlines such as "A Negro Assassin," "Assassinated by a Negro" and "SHOT HIS EMPLOYER," and in the Indianapolis Journal as "If Caught He Will Be Lynched." The Augusta dispatch appeared in the Richmond Times as "AN INFURIATED MOB. Bent on Lynching a Negro Murderer in the South," in the Washington Evening Star as "Likely to be Lynched," and in the St. Paul Daily Globe as "There May Be a Lyncncing."

Condensed versions ran in Maine, Tennessee, North Carolina, Illinois and the Dakotas into late August, some dating the shooting to the 17th. The Plaindealer, in a column otherwise given to "Afro American" and Republican news, wrote that Morrison if caught "will be dealt with after the usual Southern method," the only item to name lynching as a regional custom.

The accounts differ on what passed between the two men: the Morning News described a reproof over the mule, the Athens wire an order and an insolent reply for which Morrison was discharged, and the Augusta dispatch a "disagreeable task" followed by the shooting a few minutes later. The local correspondent's account, which placed the exchange at noon and the shooting at night, was closest to the events, though every version came from white sources.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Edmund Morrison
bases: About 100 men with bloodhounds pursued Morrison and papers said he would be lynched if caught, and he was jailed at Augusta to protect him from a mob, but no killing or attack is reported (A3, A5, A6, A8).

Morrison was not killed: he was captured by a sheriff, jailed at Augusta, tried and sentenced to hang (A5, A18); the lynching was threatened by about 100 pursuers and by Hunter's friends over the alleged killing of Hunter but not carried out (A3, A8, A9).

The Savannah Morning News's own Athens and Augusta dispatches (A1, A2, A5), the Athens wire (A3, A8) and the separate Augusta wire (A6, A9) agree on the shooting, the armed pursuit, the threat of lynching and the jailing at Augusta.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed its reports 'AN ATHENIAN SHOT BY A NEGRO', 'HUNTER'S MURDERER CAUGHT' and 'BOOKED FOR THE GIBBET' and described Morrison as 'a burly, determined villain'.

National papers ran the Athens wire under 'A Negro Assassin', 'Assassinated by a Negro', 'SHOT HIS EMPLOYER' and 'If Caught He Will Be Lynched', stating the lynching as a foregone outcome without comment.
The Augusta dispatch ran as 'AN INFURIATED MOB. Bent on Lynching a Negro Murderer in the South', 'Likely to be Lynched' and 'There May Be a Lyncncing'.
The Plaindealer's brief said Morrison if caught 'will be dealt with after the usual Southern method', naming lynching as a regional custom.
The Athens trial item praised the speed of the conviction as 'one of the quickest trials on record', run as 'A Model Court' in Clarksville.
